question: A researcher has identified a chemical compound that she expects may contribute to the development of colorectal cancer. She designs an experiment where she exposes 70 mice to a diet containing this compound with another 50 mice in a control group that was fed a regular diet. After 9 months, the mice were evaluated for tumor development at necropsy. In total, 14 mice in the experimental group developed colorectal tumor burden, and 1 mouse in the control group developed tumors. Based on this experiment, what risk of colorectal cancer can be attributable to this chemical compound?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Exposure to chemical compound -> Increased risk of colorectal cancer development -> 95% CHAIN: Experimental group exposed to compound diet -> 14 out of 70 mice developed colorectal tumors -> Control group had 1 out of 50 mice with tumors -> Suggests compound increased risk -> 90% CHAIN: Chemical compound in diet -> Higher incidence of colorectal tumors in experimental group compared to control group -> Compound contributes to cancer risk -> 85% CHAIN: Experimental group with compound diet -> 95%
analysis: The risk of colorectal cancer attributable to the chemical compound can be calculated using the formula: [(Risk in exposed group) - (Risk in unexposed group)] / (Risk in unexposed group) x 100%. In this case, the risk in the exposed group is 14/70 = 20% and the risk in the unexposed group is 1/50 = 2%. Therefore, the attributable risk is (20% - 2%) / 2% x 100% = 900%. This means that 90% of the colorectal cancer risk in the exposed group can be attributed to the chemical compound.
